recommendations.title: Reduce and monitor exposed services
recommendations.action: Inventory exposed listeners, remove unnecessary services, segment access and patch supported versions. Alert on unexpected connections; verify changes in an authorized follow-up.

references.name: Network Share Connection Removal
references.description: Adversaries may remove share connections that are no longer useful in order to clean up traces of their operation. Windows shared drive and SMB/Windows Admin Shares connections can be removed when no longer needed. Net is an example utility that can be used to remove network share connections with the net use \\system\share /delete command.

recommendations.uncertainty: Applicability requires review; this recommendation is not evidence of an implemented or effective control.

recommendations.title: Review layered preventive and detective controls
recommendations.action: Identify the assets and trust boundaries relevant to the referenced technique. Review patching, least privilege and application/security logs; assign an owner and validate chosen controls in an authorized follow-up.

references.name: Browser Information Discovery
references.description: Adversaries may enumerate information about browsers to learn more about compromised environments. Data saved by browsers (such as bookmarks, accounts, and browsing history) may reveal a variety of personal information about users (e.g., banking sites, relationships/interests, social media, etc.) as well as details about internal network resources such as servers, tools/dashboards, or other related infrastructure. Browser information may also highlight additional targets after an adversary has access to valid credentials, especially Credentials In Files associated with logins cached by a browser. Specific storage locations vary based on platform and/or application, but browser information is typically stored in local files and databases (e.g., `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`).

references.description: Adversaries may search public code repositories for information about victims that can be used during targeting. Victims may store code in repositories on various third-party websites such as GitHub, GitLab, SourceForge, and BitBucket. Users typically interact with code repositories through a web application or command-line utilities such as git. Adversaries may also identify more sensitive data, including accidentally leaked credentials or API keys.
